Celestica is an AI infrastructure supplier by its own description, and its patent record shows the work is in boards, cooling, and packaging rather than models.

The company files as a Printed Circuit Boards manufacturer on the NYSE, headquartered in Toronto. Its own profile says it engineers and manufactures infrastructure for AI, cloud, and hybrid cloud data centers. That places it upstream of the accelerators themselves, in the layer that turns chips into racks that can be powered and cooled.

The 37 granted patents point the same direction. The most recent five cover a compression device for co-packaged or near-packaged optics, a printed circuit board and wire arrangement method, a liquid cooling apparatus, an embedded multi-core upgrade method, and a fan module. Three of the five are thermal or mechanical, which is where the constraint has moved as rack densities rise. Optics packaging is the other cluster, and it matters because moving data between chips costs power that cooling then has to remove.

What the data does not show is scale. There are no revenue figures, no customer names, no backlog, and no indication of how much of this work serves AI versus other end markets. The patent count is a grant count since 2001 for one applicant phrase, not a measure of current research intensity. The filings listed are dated 2026 and establish that the company reports on a normal quarterly cadence, nothing more.
